units.title: Logic and Set
summary: A statement has exactly one truth value, T or F. Open sentences are not statements.
p wedge q is true only when both are true; p vee q is false only when both are false; p → q is false only when p is T and q is F.
p → q equiv sim p vee q equiv sim q → sim p. The converse q → p is equivalent to the inverse, not to the original.
A truth table on n letters has 2^n rows. All T = tautology, all F = contradiction, identical final columns = logical equivalence.
De Morgan, in logic and in sets: sim(p vee q) equiv sim p wedge sim q and (A ∪ B)^c = A^c ∩ B^c; (A ∩ B)^c = A^c ∪ B^c.
A - B = A ∩ B^c; n(P(A)) = 2^n(A); A = B is proved by the two inclusions A subseteq B and B subseteq A.
n(A ∪ B) = n(A)+n(B)-n(A ∩ B) and n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = Σ n(A) - Σ n(A ∩ B) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).

units.title: Real Numbers
summary: mathbbN ⊂ mathbbW ⊂ mathbbZ ⊂ mathbbQ ⊂ mathbbR; a real number is rational iff its decimal terminates or recurs.
Each real number corresponds to exactly one point of the number line and conversely; √n is located exactly by a Pythagorean construction.
Between any two distinct reals there are infinitely many rationals and infinitely many irrationals.
(a,b) excludes endpoints, [a,b] includes them; ∞ always takes a round bracket; the length of either is b-a.
|x| = x for x ≥ 0 and -x for x < 0; |x| = √x^2; |x-y| is the distance from x to y.
|x| < k Leftrightarrow -k < x < k (one interval); |x| > k Leftrightarrow x < -k or x > k (two intervals).
Triangle inequality |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b|; a sum of two moduli is solved by splitting the line at the zeros of each inside expression.

units.title: Functions
summary: f : A → B assigns exactly one image to each element of A; the range f(A) may be a proper subset of the co-domain B.
One-one means distinct inputs have distinct images; onto means range = co-domain; a bijection is both, and only a bijection is invertible.
Domain rules: no division by zero, no even root of a negative, no log of a non-positive number; take the intersection when several apply.
(g ° f)(x) = g(f(x)) — apply f first. In general f ° g ≠ g ° f, and (f ° g)^-1 = g^-1 ° f^-1.
To invert: write y = f(x), make x the subject, swap letters. Domain and range swap, and the graph of f^-1 is the reflection of that of f in y = x.
Quadratic y = ax^2+bx+c: vertex at x = -(b)/(2a), opens up if a>0; the number of x-intercepts is decided by b^2-4ac.
sin x, cos x: domain mathbbR, range [-1,1], period 2π; tan x: range mathbbR, period π.
a^x: domain mathbbR, range (0,∞), through (0,1). loga x: domain (0,∞), range mathbbR, through (1,0). They are mutual inverses.

topics: Symmetry about origin, X-axis and Y-axis; monotonicity
Graphs of quadratic, cubic, rational function of form 1/(ax+b)

sections.title: Symmetry about origin, X-axis and Y-axis; monotonicity
Graphs of quadratic, cubic, rational function of form 1/(ax+b)
Graphs of asin bx, acos bx, e^x, ln x

summary: f is even if f(-x) = f(x) (graph symmetric about the Y-axis) and odd if f(-x) = -f(x) (symmetric about the origin). odd × odd = even.
f is periodic with period T if f(x+T) = f(x); asin bx and acos bx have period (2π)/(|b|), and atan bx has period (π)/(|b|).
Symmetry tests: x → -x unchanged gives Y-axis symmetry; y → -y gives X-axis symmetry; both together give origin symmetry.
f is increasing on I if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) < f(x2); prove it from the sign of f(x2)-f(x1). Monotonicity is claimed on an interval, never pointwise.
Quadratic: vertex at x = -(b)/(2a), opens up if a>0; number of x-intercepts from the discriminant b^2-4ac.
y = (1)/(ax+b): vertical asymptote x = -(b)/(a), horizontal asymptote y = 0, y-intercept (1)/(b), no x-intercept, two decreasing branches when a>0, range mathbbR-0.
y = asin bx: amplitude |a|, period (2π)/(|b|), range [-|a|,|a|]; acos bx is the same curve starting at its maximum.
e^x: domain mathbbR, range (0,∞), through (0,1), asymptote y=0. ln x: domain (0,∞), range mathbbR, through (1,0), asymptote x=0.

units.title: Sequence and Series
topics: Arithmetic, geometric and harmonic sequences and series
A.M., G.M., H.M. and their relations

sections.title: Arithmetic, geometric and harmonic sequences and series
A.M., G.M., H.M. and their relations

summary: AP: tn = a+(n-1)d and Sn = (n)/(2)[2a+(n-1)d] = (n)/(2)(a+l). Three terms are in AP if 2b = a+c.
GP: tn = ar^ n-1 and Sn = dfraca(r^n-1)r-1 = dfraca(1-r^n)1-r for r ≠ 1. Three terms are in GP if b^2 = ac.
HP: reciprocals form an AP, so tn = 1/[a+(n-1)d]. Invert, solve as an AP, invert back. There is no elementary sum formula.
Means of a and b: A = dfraca+b2, G = √ab, H = dfrac2aba+b.
G^2 = AH (so A, G, H are in GP) and A ≥ G ≥ H, with equality only when a = b.
Inserting n means makes n+2 terms: d = dfracb-an+1, r = (b/a)^1/(n+1).
Sum to infinity: S∞ = dfraca1-r if and only if |r| < 1.
Two given facts about a sequence give two equations: subtract them for an AP, divide them for a GP.

units.title: Matrices and Determinants
topics: Transpose of a matrix and its properties
Adjoint and inverse of a matrix

sections.title: Transpose of a matrix and its properties
Adjoint and inverse of a matrix

summary: (AB)ij is row i of A against column j of B; AB needs (columns of A) = (rows of B), and AB ≠ BA in general.
Transpose swaps rows and columns: (A^T)^T = A, (A+B)^T = A^T+B^T, (kA)^T = kA^T, and the reversal law (AB)^T = B^TA^T.
Symmetric: A^T = A. Skew-symmetric: A^T = -A (zero diagonal). Every square A = frac12(A+A^T) + frac12(A-A^T).
Minor Mij = determinant after deleting row i and column j; cofactor Cij = (-1)^i+jMij. Expand |A| along the row or column with most zeros.
adj A = transpose of the cofactor matrix, and A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A|I.
A^-1 = dfracadj A|A| exists iff |A| ≠ 0; (AB)^-1 = B^-1A^-1 and |A^-1| = 1/|A|.
Determinant properties: |A^T| = |A|; a row swap flips the sign; equal or proportional rows give 0; |kA| = k^n|A|; adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing; |AB| = |A||B|.
Systems: AX = B gives X = A^-1B; Cramer's rule gives x = Dx/D etc. for D ≠ 0; Gauss elimination row-reduces the augmented matrix to upper-triangular form and back-substitutes.

units.title: Quadratic Equation
topics: Symmetric roots; one or both roots common

sections.title: Symmetric roots; one or both roots common

summary: ax^2+bx+c = 0 has roots x = dfrac-b±√b^2-4ac2a.
Discriminant D = b^2-4ac: D > 0 real distinct (D a perfect square makes them rational), D = 0 real and equal, D < 0 a conjugate complex pair.
α+β = -b/a and αβ = c/a; and (α-β)^2 = D/a^2.
Useful identities: α^2+β^2 = s^2-2p, α^3+β^3 = s^3-3ps, dfrac1α+dfrac1β = dfracsp.
To form an equation: x^2 - (sum)x + (product) = 0.
Symmetric expressions in the roots can always be written in s and p; α-β cannot, so it carries a ±.
One root common: substitute the known roots of one equation into the other; in general (c1a2-c2a1)^2 = (a1b2-a2b1)(b1c2-b2c1).
Both roots common: dfraca1a2 = dfracb1b2 = dfracc1c2.

sections.title: Imaginary unit; algebra of complex numbers

summary: i = √-1, i^2 = -1; powers of i repeat with period 4.
z = a+ib; a+ib = c+id exactly when a = c and b = d.
Divide by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
Argand diagram: z = a+ib is the point (a,b); |z| = √a^2+b^2 and arg z = θ with tanθ = b/a, fixed by the quadrant.
Polar form z = r(cosθ + isinθ).
z = a-ib; zz = |z|^2, z+z = 2 Re(z), z-z = 2i Im(z), dfrac1z = dfracz|z|^2.
Cube roots of unity: 1, ω, ω^2 with ω^3 = 1 and 1+ω+ω^2 = 0.

units.title: Inverse Circular Functions
topics: Definition, domain and range of inverse circular functions
Formulae and identities of inverse circular functions

sections.title: Definition, domain and range of inverse circular functions
Formulae and identities of inverse circular functions

summary: Inverse circular functions exist only after the domain is restricted to a one-to-one principal branch; the graph of the inverse is the reflection of that branch in y=x.
Ranges: sin^-1, csc^-1 ∈left[-(π)/(2),(π)/(2)right]; tan^-1∈left(-(π)/(2),(π)/(2)right); cos^-1, sec^-1∈[0,π]; cot^-1∈(0,π).
sin^-1x+cos^-1x = tan^-1x+cot^-1x = sec^-1x+csc^-1x = (π)/(2).
sin^-1(-x)=-sin^-1x and tan^-1(-x)=-tan^-1x, but cos^-1(-x)=π-cos^-1x and cot^-1(-x)=π-cot^-1x.
tan^-1x+tan^-1y = tan^-1(x+y)/(1-xy) if xy<1; add π if x,y>0 with xy>1 and subtract π if x,y<0 with xy>1.
sin^-1x+sin^-1y = sin^-1left(x√1-y^2+y√1-x^2right) and cos^-1x+cos^-1y = cos^-1left(xy-√1-x^2√1-y^2right).
sin^-1(sin x)=x only for x∈left[-(π)/(2),(π)/(2)right]; otherwise shift the angle into the range first.

units.title: Trigonometric Equations and General Values
summary: A trigonometric equation has infinitely many roots; the answer required is the general value, with n∈mathbbZ stated.
sinθ=sinα ⇒ θ = nπ+(-1)^nα; cosθ=cosα ⇒ θ = 2nπ±α; tanθ=tanα ⇒ θ = nπ+α.
Squared equations sin^2θ=sin^2α (and the cos^2, tan^2 versions) all give θ = nπ±α.
Zero cases: sinθ=0 ⇒ θ=nπ; cosθ=0 ⇒ θ=(2n+1)(π)/(2); tanθ=0 ⇒ θ=nπ.
Quadratics in one ratio: factorise. Mixed sin^2/cos: substitute sin^2θ = 1-cos^2θ. Sums of sines or cosines: use sum-to-product, then factorise.
acosθ+bsinθ = c becomes rcos(θ-α)=c with r=√a^2+b^2, tanα = b/a; solvable only if |c|≤ r.
Never cancel a common trigonometric factor — factorise and set each factor to zero. Always reject roots that need |sinθ|>1 or |cosθ|>1.

topics: Length of perpendicular from a given point to a given line
Bisectors of the angles between two straight lines

sections.title: Length of perpendicular from a given point to a given line
Bisectors of the angles between two straight lines

summary: General form ax+by+c=0; slope m = -a/b = tanθ where θ is the inclination. Forms: y=mx+c, y-y1=m(x-x1), x/a+y/b=1, xcosα+ysinα=p.
Angle between two lines: tanθ = |dfracm1-m21+m1m2|; parallel if m1=m2, perpendicular if m1m2=-1 or a1a2+b1b2=0.
Perpendicular distance from (x1,y1) to ax+by+c=0: d = dfrac|ax1+by1+c|√a^2+b^2; from the origin, d = dfrac|c|√a^2+b^2 = p.
Distance between the parallel lines ax+by+c1=0 and ax+by+c2=0 is dfrac|c1-c2|√a^2+b^2, after making a and b identical.
The bisectors of the angles between two lines are dfraca1x+b1y+c1√a1^2+b1^2 = ±dfraca2x+b2y+c2√a2^2+b2^2, and they are perpendicular to each other.
With c1,c2>0: the + sign gives the bisector of the angle containing the origin; that angle is acute when a1a2+b1b2<0.
A bisector can always be identified by testing whether tanθ<1 for the angle it makes with one of the original lines.

topics: General equation of second degree; condition for representing a pair of lines
Homogeneous second degree equation in x and y

sections.title: General equation of second degree; condition for representing a pair of lines

summary: ax^2+2hxy+by^2+2gx+2fy+c = 0 represents a pair of straight lines exactly when Δ = abc+2fgh-af^2-bg^2-ch^2 = 0. Remember h, g, f are half the coefficients of xy, x, y.
The lines are real and distinct if h^2>ab, coincident if h^2=ab, parallel if h^2=ab with the pair not degenerate, and not real if h^2<ab.
They meet at left(dfracbg-fhh^2-ab, dfracaf-ghh^2-abright).
A homogeneous equation ax^2+2hxy+by^2 = 0 always represents two lines through the origin, with m1+m2 = -dfrac2hb and m1m2 = dfracab.
Angle between the pair: tanθ = dfrac2√h^2-aba+b; they are perpendicular when a+b = 0 and coincident when h^2 = ab.
The pair through the origin perpendicular to ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0 is bx^2-2hxy+ay^2 = 0.
The bisectors of the angles between the pair are dfracx^2-y^2a-b = dfracxyh; they are always perpendicular to each other.
To find the lines joining the origin to the intersections of lx+my=n with a curve, homogenise the curve using dfraclx+myn = 1.

units.title: Coordinates in Space
summary: Three mutually perpendicular axes give three coordinate planes (x=0, y=0, z=0) and eight octants; a point is an ordered triple (x,y,z).
Distance of P(x,y,z) from the xy-plane is |z|; from the x-axis is √y^2+z^2; from the origin is √x^2+y^2+z^2.

Section formula (internal, ratio m:n): left(dfracmx2+nx1m+n, dfracmy2+ny1m+n, dfracmz2+nz1m+nright); for external division replace n by -n. Midpoint is the case m=n; centroid is the average of the three vertices.
Direction cosines l = cosα, m = cosβ, n = cosγ satisfy l^2+m^2+n^2 = 1, and l = dfracxr, m = dfracyr, n = dfraczr with r = OP.
Direction ratios (a,b,c) are any numbers proportional to (l,m,n); divide by √a^2+b^2+c^2 to get the direction cosines.
The join of A and B has direction ratios (x2-x1, y2-y1, z2-z1).
cosθ = l1l2+m1m2+n1n2; lines are perpendicular when a1a2+b1b2+c1c2 = 0 and parallel when their direction ratios are proportional.

units.title: Vectors

sections.title: The scalar product and the angle between two vectors

summary: A vector needs magnitude and direction; in components r = xi+yj+zk with |r| = √x^2+y^2+z^2, unit vector r = r/|r|, and direction cosines satisfying l^2+m^2+n^2 = 1.
Triangle law: AB+BC = AC. For two vectors at angle θ, R = √a^2+b^2+2abcosθ and tanα = dfracbsinθa+bcosθ.
AB = b-a (head minus tail) — the key to every proof.
Collinear: a = kb; points A,B,C collinear if BC = k AB.
Section formula: internal r = dfracmb+nam+n, external r = dfracmb-nam-n, midpoint dfraca+b2.
Coplanar: c = xa+yb; two non-collinear vectors span a plane and three non-coplanar vectors span space, with unique coefficients.
Linearly dependent means c1a1+cdots+cnan = 0 with the ci not all zero. Two vectors: dependent = collinear. Three: dependent = coplanar.
acdotb = |a||b|cosθ = a1b1+a2b2+a3b3; acdotb = 0 Leftrightarrow perpendicular; projection of b on a is acdotb/|a|.

units.title: Measures of Dispersion
topics: Skewness; Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness

sections.title: Skewness; Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness

summary: Dispersion measures spread about the average. Range = L-S; Q.D. = (Q3-Q1)/(2); M.D. = (Σ| x-x|)/(n).
Variance σ^2 = dfracΣ(x-x)^2n = dfracΣ x^2n - x^2; standard deviation σ = √σ^2, in the original unit.
Frequency data: x = dfracΣ fxN and σ = √dfracΣ fx^2N - x^2 with N = Σ f.
Grouped data (step deviation, d' = (x-A)/(h)): x = A + dfracΣ fd'Nh and σ = h√dfracΣ fd'^2N - left(dfracΣ fd'Nright)^2.
σ is unchanged by adding a constant and multiplied by | k| when every value is multiplied by k.
Combined SD: σ12 = √dfracn1(σ1^2+d1^2) + n2(σ2^2+d2^2)n1+n2 with di = xi - x12.
C.V. = dfracσx×100%: smaller C.V. = more consistent. Use it whenever the means or the units differ.
Skewness measures lopsidedness: Sk = dfracx-Moσ = dfrac3(x-Md)σ, with Mo = 3Md - 2x as the empirical link.

units.title: Probability
topics: Mathematical and empirical definition of probability
Two basic laws of probability (without proof)

sections.title: Mathematical and empirical definition of probability

summary: A random experiment has a sample space S; an event is a subset of S. Cases may be exhaustive, equally likely, mutually exclusive (A∩ B = varnothing) or independent (one does not affect the other).
Mathematical definition: P(A) = dfracn(A)n(S) = dfracmn, valid only for equally likely cases. 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1 and P(A) = 1 - P(A).
Empirical definition: P(A) = limn→∞ dfracmn, the limiting relative frequency in repeated trials.
Odds in favour a:b Longleftrightarrow P(A) = dfracaa+b.
Addition law: P(A∪ B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩ B); for mutually exclusive events P(A∪ B) = P(A)+P(B).
Multiplication law: P(A∩ B) = P(A)P(B|A); for independent events P(A∩ B) = P(A)P(B). Conditional probability P(B|A) = dfracP(A∩ B)P(A).
For two dice n(S) = 36; for n coins n(S) = 2^n; for a pack of cards n(S) = 52 with 4 suits of 13, 12 face cards and 26 red.
"At least one" = 1 - P(none). Draw a tree for multi-stage problems: multiply along a branch, add across branches.

units.title: Limits and Continuity
topics: Concept of limit; limits of algebraic and transcendental functions
Continuity and discontinuity of a function

sections.title: Concept of limit; limits of algebraic and transcendental functions
Continuity and discontinuity of a function

summary: limx→ af(x) = L describes the behaviour of f near a, never at a; the value f(a) is irrelevant to the limit.
The limit exists iff LHL = RHL = L, finite. Use x = a mp h, h>0, to compute one-sided limits.
Formally: for every varepsilon>0 there is δ>0 with 0<|x-a|<δ ⇒ |f(x)-L|<varepsilon.
Standard limits: (x^n-a^n)/(x-a)→ na^n-1; (sin x)/(x)→1; (tan x)/(x)→1; frac1-cos xx^2→frac12; (1+x)^1/x→ e; fraca^x-1x→ln a; (ln(1+x))/(x)→1; frac1x^n→0 as x→∞.
The six indeterminate forms are frac00, (∞)/(∞), ∞-∞, 0×∞, 1^∞, 0^0 (with ∞^0). Factorise, rationalise, divide by the highest power, or force the e form.
For a rational function as x→∞: bottom heavier ⇒ 0; equal degrees ⇒ ratio of leading coefficients; top heavier ⇒∞.
f is continuous at a iff limx→ a^-f = limx→ a^+f = f(a).
Discontinuities are removable (limit exists, value wrong or missing), jump (finite unequal one-sided limits) or infinite (a one-sided limit is ±∞, giving a vertical asymptote).

units.title: Derivatives
topics: Derivatives of parametric and implicit functions
Monotonicity of a function; intervals of increase and decrease

sections.title: Derivatives of parametric and implicit functions
Monotonicity of a function; intervals of increase and decrease

summary: First principle: f'(x) = limh→0dfracf(x+h)-f(x)h. Four steps — form f(x+h), subtract, divide by h, take the limit. The trick in step 2 is expansion (polynomials), the conjugate (surds), a common denominator (fractions), sum-to-product (trigonometric) or a standard limit (exponential and logarithmic).
Differentiable ⇒ continuous, but not the reverse: |x| has a corner at 0 where the left and right derivatives are -1 and +1.
Rules: (u± v)' = u'± v'; (uv)' = uv'+vu'; left(frac uvright)' = fracvu'-uv'v^2; chain rule (dy)/(dx) = (dy)/(du)·(du)/(dx).

Standard derivatives: x^n → nx^n-1; e^x → e^x; a^x → a^xln a; ln x → 1/x; sin x → cos x; cos x → -sin x; tan x → sec^2x; sin^-1x → 1/√1-x^2; tan^-1x → 1/(1+x^2). Every "co-" function carries a minus sign.
Logarithmic differentiation for [f(x)]^g(x) and for long products/quotients: take ln of both sides, then differentiate, remembering (d)/(dx)ln y = frac1y(dy)/(dx).

Implicit: differentiate every term in x, attaching (dy)/(dx) to each y-term, then collect and factor. Parametric: (dy)/(dx) = dfracdy/dtdx/dt, and fracd^2ydx^2 = dfrac(d)/(dt)left((dy)/(dx)right)dx/dt — never ddot y/ddot x.
Geometry: f'(a) is the slope of the tangent at x=a; the normal has slope -1/f'(a); the angle between curves is tanθ = left|dfracm1-m21+m1m2right|.

Monotonicity: f' > 0 increasing, f' < 0 decreasing. Extremes: solve f' = 0, then use the sign change of f' or the sign of f'' (f''<0 maximum, f''>0 minimum). On a closed interval, test the endpoints too.

units.title: Anti-derivatives
topics: Area under a curve; area between two curves

sections.title: Area under a curve; area between two curves

summary: ∫ f(x)dx = F(x)+C means F'(x)=f(x). The constant C is compulsory in an indefinite integral and cancels in a definite one.
Integration is linear: constants come out, sums split. There is no product or quotient rule.
Standard forms to know cold: ∫ x^n dx = fracx^n+1n+1 (n≠-1), ∫(dx)/(x)=ln|x|, ∫(dx)/(a^2+x^2)=frac1atan^-1(x)/(a), ∫fracdx√a^2-x^2=sin^-1(x)/(a), ∫(dx)/(x^2-a^2)=(1)/(2a)ln(|x-a|)/(|x+a|).
Substitution: u=g(x), du=g'(x)dx. Two workhorses: ∫(f')/(f)dx=ln|f|+C and ∫ f^n f'dx = fracf^n+1n+1+C. Surds √a^2-x^2, √a^2+x^2, √x^2-a^2 call for x=asinθ, atanθ, asecθ.
Quadratic denominators: complete the square; for (px+q)/(ax^2+bx+c) write px+q=λ(2ax+b)+μ. Rational functions: divide if improper, then split into partial fractions by the four denominator cases.
By parts: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du, choosing u by ILATE. Apply twice for x^2 factors; for ∫ e^axsin bx dx apply twice and solve for I.
∫a^b f(x)dx = limn→∞hΣr=1^nf(a+rh) with h=(b-a)/(n), and equals F(b)-F(a) by the fundamental theorem. Change the limits whenever you change the variable.
Useful properties: ∫0^a f(x)dx=∫0^a f(a-x)dx; ∫-a^af=2∫0^a f for even f and 0 for odd f.

units.title: Computational Methods
topics: Roots of algebraic and transcendental equations: bisection method

sections.title: Roots of algebraic and transcendental equations: bisection method
Extension: linear programming by the graphical method

summary: A root of f(x)=0 is bracketed whenever f(a) f(b) < 0 and f is continuous on [a,b].

Bisection: repeatedly take c = (a+b)/(2) and keep the half in which the sign change lies. It always converges, and |xn-α| ≤ fracb-a2^n, so n > (ln((b-a)/varepsilon))/(ln 2) iterations guarantee accuracy varepsilon.

Newton-Raphson: xn+1 = xn - fracf(xn)f'(xn), obtained by replacing the curve with its tangent. Convergence is quadratic (correct digits double each step) but is not guaranteed; it fails when f'(xn) is zero or the start is poor.
Special cases: xn+1 = frac12left(xn+fracNxnright) for √N, and xn+1 = (1)/(3)left(2xn+fracNxn^2right) for √[3]N.
Trapezoidal rule with h = (b-a)/(n): ∫a^bf dx ≈ (h)/(2)left[(y0+yn)+2(y1+cdots+yn-1)right], with |ET| ≤ frac(b-a)h^212M2. Any n is allowed.

Simpson's one-third rule (n even): ∫a^bf dx ≈ (h)/(3)left[(y0+yn)+4(odd y)+2(even y)right], with |ES| ≤ frac(b-a)h^4180M4. Simpson's three-eighths rule uses (3h)/(8) with coefficients 1,3,3,2,3,3,ldots,1 and needs n a multiple of three.
Simpson's rule is exact for any cubic; the trapezoidal rule is exact only for a straight line and always errs to the same side of a curve of fixed concavity.
In a linear programming problem the optimum of Z = ax+by occurs at a corner of the feasible region, so evaluate Z at every vertex and compare.

summary: A force is a vector: magnitude, direction, point of application. Forces at a point are concurrent; forces in one plane are coplanar.
Parallelogram law: two forces P, Q at angle θ have resultant R = √P^2+Q^2+2PQcosθ making angle α = tan^-1dfracQsinθP+Qcosθ with P.
The resultant always lies between |P-Q| and P+Q; it equals P+Q at θ = 0^°, √P^2+Q^2 at 90^°, |P-Q| at 180^°.
Resolution: Fx = Fcosθ, Fy = Fsinθ. Any number of coplanar concurrent forces combine as X = Σ Fcosθ, Y = Σ Fsinθ, R = √X^2+Y^2, tanθ = Y/X; read the quadrant from the signs.
Equilibrium Leftrightarrow X = 0 and Y = 0. For three forces use Lami's theorem: each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two is the same. The equilibrant is minus the resultant.
Kinematics: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt = d^2s/dt^2. Distance is not displacement; reverse of direction happens where v changes sign.
Uniform acceleration only: v = u+at, s = ut+tfrac12 at^2, v^2 = u^2+2as, s = tfrac12(u+v)t, and sn = u + tfraca(2n-1)2. On a v–t graph the gradient is a and the area is s.
Gravity: a = -g upwards positive, a = +g downwards positive, with g = 9.8 m/s^2. Maximum height u^2/2g, time of flight 2u/g.
